dimensions.evidence: The opening section is entirely forward-looking design intent plus an exclusion list: "Success means a user can request work, resume it, or check it with the single skill; setup previews all writes before approval; declared risk never falls; changed paths can require explicit upward escalation; dated records and decision references remain valid; a saved handoff does not alter the diff digest; and doctor/hooks disclose no secrets or home paths." Every item is a property the change was built to have, asserted as satisfied. The remainder is "Non-goals are TDD, planning, product review, automatic releases, autonomous loops, mandatory comments, or generalized host adapters" — the deferred/excluded-feature list the dimension explicitly disqualifies. I searched the opening section for any statement of confidence, residual uncertainty, an expectation that might not hold, or a criterion whose outcome was open (e.g. 'we expected', 'may not', 'unknown whether') and found none; a reader who stopped after this section would proceed identically no matter what the rest of the record reported.

No check is named with a result. The closest candidates are mitigations, not checks: "Path validation, upward-only risk, no-op activation, exit-zero hook behavior, bounded redacted diagnostics, and Git-ignored handoffs address these risks" — a list of designed behaviors, with no statement that any was exercised or what it produced. "The bundled CLI reads the validated contract and evidence" describes runtime behavior, not a verification performed. The section titled "Existing responsibilities searched" reports a conclusion ("remain their canonical owners") without naming what was searched or what the search returned. I searched all five graded sections for a test run, script invocation, manual trial, review, or judge run together with its outcome and found none.

The central argument rests on these undefined terms: (1) "diff digest" — load-bearing in "Verification results remain bound to the current diff digest" and "a saved handoff does not alter the diff digest", with no statement of what it digests or when it changes; (2) "contract" and "contract classifier" — "The bundled CLI reads the validated contract and evidence" and "validates the contract", never said what a contract is or what validation means; (3) "evidence" / "evidence validator" — used as the object bound to verification, undefined; (4) "declared risk", "path-detected", and "explicit risk" — "computes effective risk as the maximum of declared, path-detected, and explicit risk" defines the combination but none of the three inputs, while "declared risk never falls" and "upward-only risk" are stated as the security guarantee; (5) "Briefs" — "Framework outputs remain canonical in their own repositories and are linked from Briefs"; (6) "the shared skill router" and "shared Agent Skill"; (7) "advise-only check" and "bounded status" — "SessionStart reads bounded status; Stop runs advise-only check", where the safety claim "Neither path invokes `verify`" depends on knowing what these do; (8) "v0.2-only commands", the entire rollback unit in "Rollback is removal of hook declarations and v0.2-only commands". The list is non-empty, so D3 fails.

The three takeaway candidates are all general properties or scope disclaimers. "Plugin hosts may disable or decline trust for hooks; the skill and CLI must remain sufficient" states a general property of third-party plugin hosts with no observation from this change that produced it — nothing says a host was seen declining trust, or under what circumstance. "`doctor` can only report whether host plugin listings expose the package and does not prove implicit skill selection quality" is the disqualified "X does not cover Y" form. "The setup preview is agent behavior described by the skill, not an autonomous CLI configuration detector" is likewise a scope correction. I searched all five sections for an observation a reader could make that would overturn any transferable claim, and for any conditional of the form 'this stops holding when…', and found none.

graders.rubric_feedback: Three concerns. (1) D3 is close to unpassable for any record that names its own artifacts. Its exemption requires each term's role to be stated in the sentence that uses it, but a record describing a system with a dozen domain nouns would have to inline-define all of them or write so abstractly the nouns disappear — and abstraction is the failure D3 exists to catch. Because the list is the verdict, a record with one borderline term fails identically to one that is wholly opaque, so D3 cannot distinguish 'dense but internally consistent' from 'unreadable'. Consider capping it at terms the central claim cannot survive without, or scoring by count. (2) D1 asks the judge to read only the opening section, but 'could plausibly have resolved the other way' is not decidable from that section alone. Here "a saved handoff does not alter the diff digest" looks like a mere designed property in isolation, and only the later line "handoff writes invalidating evidence" reveals it was a live risk. The verdict therefore turns on how much the judge already knows about which invariants are hard — the exact outside knowledge the 'new engineer' framing is meant to remove. (3) D2 is satisfiable without doing the work: 'we ran the test suite and it passed' names a check and its outcome and passes, regardless of whether that check bears on any claim the record makes. A clearly bad record — vague, unfalsifiable, jargon-defined — clears D2 by appending one sentence about a lint run. D2 would be stronger if the check had to bear on a specific claim made elsewhere in the record.

dimensions.evidence: The opening section is a specification plus an exclusion list: "Success means a user can request work, resume it, or check it with the single skill; setup previews all writes before approval; declared risk never falls; changed paths can require explicit upward escalation; dated records and decision references remain valid; a saved handoff does not alter the diff digest; and doctor/hooks disclose no secrets or home paths." and "Non-goals are TDD, planning, product review, automatic releases, autonomous loops, mandatory comments, or generalized host adapters." Every one of the seven criteria is a property the change was built to supply, and each is paired later with the mechanism that supplies it — "Git-ignored handoffs", "bounded redacted diagnostics", "upward-only risk". I searched the section for a criterion stating a proposition that could plausibly have resolved the other way, and for any statement of confidence, uncertainty, or residual doubt; there is none. A reader who stopped after this section would decide the same way no matter what the rest of the record reported.

I searched all five sections for a sentence reporting something that was run, tested, measured, or observed, together with its outcome — words in the family of ran, tested, verified, confirmed, observed, found, produced. The nearest candidates are descriptions of mechanism, not of a check performed: "Verification results remain bound to the current diff digest" and "Path validation, upward-only risk, no-op activation, exit-zero hook behavior, bounded redacted diagnostics, and Git-ignored handoffs address these risks." The section headed "Existing responsibilities searched" reports a conclusion — "The existing CLI parser, evidence validator, repository-safe write helper, contract classifier, templates, diff digest, shared Agent Skill, release builder, and plugin manifests remain their canonical owners" — without naming what was searched or what the search returned. No check is named anywhere, so no check's result is stated.

Undefined terms the central argument rests on, each load-bearing and none given a role in the sentence that uses it: "diff digest" (the safety claim "a saved handoff does not alter the diff digest" and the freshness claim "Verification results remain bound to the current diff digest" both turn on it); "declared", "path-detected", and "explicit" risk in "computes effective risk as the maximum of declared, path-detected, and explicit risk" (the composite is defined, the three inputs are not); "contract" in "reads the validated contract"; "evidence" in "handoff writes invalidating evidence"; "Briefs" in "Framework outputs remain canonical in their own repositories and are linked from Briefs"; "shared skill router" and "shared Agent Skill"; "upward escalation" / "upward-only risk"; "v0.2-only commands" in the rollback claim "Rollback is removal of hook declarations and v0.2-only commands". A new engineer cannot judge whether the rollback is safe, whether risk truly never falls, or whether a handoff is harmless without resolving these elsewhere. The list is non-empty.

The candidate transferable claim is "Plugin hosts may disable or decline trust for hooks; the skill and CLI must remain sufficient" — a general property of third-party plugin hosts, stated without any observation from this change that produced it (no host is named, no decline was encountered, no consequence was seen). The other two items are scope disclaimers, which the dimension excludes: "`doctor` can only report whether host plugin listings expose the package and does not prove implicit skill selection quality" and "The setup preview is agent behavior described by the skill, not an autonomous CLI configuration detector." I searched for a condition naming an observation a reader could make that would overturn the claim — a symptom, a host behavior, a threshold — and found none.

graders.rubric_feedback:
D1's disqualifier is the weakest joint. 'Properties the change was built to have' describes nearly every success criterion ever written, so the whole verdict rests on the escape clause 'could plausibly have resolved the other way' — and that is a fact about the author's prior state of belief, which the text does not carry. Two criteria here, 'a saved handoff does not alter the diff digest' and 'doctor/hooks disclose no secrets or home paths', read equally well as design guarantees and as empirical claims that could have failed; I resolved them against the record only because the later section names a mechanism supplying each. A record that phrased the same built-in guarantees as risky-sounding propositions, and omitted the mechanisms, would pass D1 having done no additional work. Consider requiring the opening section to state what was still uncertain at the time of writing, or what observation would have made the change unsuccessful — something whose absence is visible in the text rather than inferable from the author's confidence.

D2 has an unstated boundary that this record sits directly on. A section titled 'Existing responsibilities searched' asserts a search, and reports a finding (which components own what). The dimension does not say whether a code search with stated findings counts as 'a check' — it addresses tests, judge runs, and scripts. I read it as not a check, since neither the query nor the result of searching is given, only a conclusion about ownership. But a record could satisfy a lenient reader of D2 by writing 'searched for parallel implementations, found none' — a sentence costing nothing and verifying nothing. Worth stating explicitly whether a search counts, and if so what its stated output must contain.

D3's exemption ('in-repo identifiers whose role is stated in the sentence that uses them') is clear, but leaves a gap for config keys and enum values: `automation.session_hooks` set to `remind` has its effect stated in place ('exits immediately unless…'), while its meaning does not. I excluded it from the list on that basis. Since D3 fails on a non-empty list, borderline items are cheap for a judge to include and inflate the verdict's apparent strength; the dimension might ask for the two or three most load-bearing terms rather than an exhaustive list.
